Douglas:

The graphical user interface to Distance limits the number of model
definitions to 5.  However, if you look at the Log window, you can see a
set of commands in the MCDS command language like this:

  Estimate;
  Distance;
  Density=All;
  Encounter=All;
  Detection=All;
  Size=All;
  Estimator /Key=HN /Adjust=CO /Criterion=AIC;
  Estimator /Key=HN /Adjust=PO /Criterion=AIC;
  Estimator /Key=UN /Adjust=PO /Criterion=AIC;
  Estimator /Key=HA /Adjust=PO /Criterion=AIC;
  Estimator /Key=HA /Adjust=CO /Criterion=AIC;
  Monotone=Strict;
  Pick=AIC;

These lines are created by the graphical interface.  If you need more
models, you can alter the commands (specifying more models) run MCDS
from the command line of your operating system.  This process, if you
are adept at working directly with the operating system from the command
line, is explained in the Users Guide appendix entitled: MCDS Engine
Reference.

Fundamentally you will be running the Fortran program MCDS directly with
a command such as

"C:\Program Files\Distance6\MCDS" 0, "C:\Temp\Input File.txt"

That is the technical answer to your question.  My experience has been
that for reasonable data, competing models with small delta-AIC values
produce very similar density estimates.  To have small differences in
delta-AIC but large differences in estimated density is an unusual
situation and may indicate problems with the data.

messages.subject: Re: Which truncation is best?
messages.body_plain:
All good questions Delyth:

As you probably know, there is no perfect answer to the question "what
is the proper truncation distance"?

Happy you consulted the archives to discover what the monotonicity
warning was about and that you took action to truncate detections that
caused there to be a rise in detections at large distances.

The heart of the matter is what to do about "parameter 2 is at a
bound".  That warning is cause for concern because it suggests that the
hazard rate function that fitted best was one in which the beta
coefficient (pp 46-47 of Buckland et al. (2001)) was as small as
Distance permitted.  That is usually an indication of an unreliable
estimate.

Look at many of the example histograms in Chapter 4 of Buckland et al.
(2001): Fig 4.1, 4.4, 4.5; all have bars that exceed 1.0. Remember the
histograms are of a sample of perpendicular distances. Distance is
attempting to fit data that best describe the process by which
detectability diminishes as a function of perpendicular distance.  Do
not be terribly concerned about occasional bins above 1.

One diagnostic you have not mentioned is goodness-of-fit.  Include that
consideration in your decision process regarding model choice.

messages.subject_clean: Sampling effort in post stratified data
messages.body_plain:
Fernanda:

Glad to see you are using what we discussed in Cambridge.

The most common way to think about stratification is geographic: stratum
1 is over there, stratum 2 is over here.  Sampling effort is allocated
within geographical strata. When post-stratifying, Distance allocates
effort to each strata; in your case sex.  Of course you do not
repeatedly walk transects for each sex.  If the factor you were
post-stratifying upon had 3 categories, it would appear as if your
effort had trebled.

Distance is performing the proper calculations: encounter rates (number
of detections [by sex] per unit of transect walked) is calculated
correctly.  No need for you to alter your data input.

messages.subject: Re: Multipliers or multiplying transect length?
messages.body_plain:
Delyth:

My opinion is that multiplying the line length by the number of visits
is a more accurate representation of what took place.  The effort you
expended is measured in kilometres walked which is equal to line length
times number of transits of those lines.

Distance knows nothing about the identity of the individuals you
encountered.  Repeated sightings of animals by walking the same transect
twice does not affect the point estimate of density.  If you look at the
formula for estimating density you will see embedded inside it the ratio
(n/L) detections divided by effort.  This is called the encounter rate.

Imagine you are trying to estimate density of trees in the desert and
there is only a single tree in the desert.  You choose to only place one
transect in your desert of length 1km, and that transect happens to be
sufficiently close to the tree that you detect it from this transect.
If you walk the transect once (and detect your tree), the encounter rate
is 1/1km.  If you walk the transect a second time (and detect the tree
again), the effort doubles to 2km, but the detections also double,
leaving the encounter rate at 2/2km=1/1km.

What is missing from this story is the variability of that encounter
rate.  We would like to know how representative the places we visit is
of the entire desert.   Well, by having but a single transect, we do not
know how variable this encounter rate is throughout the desert.
Likewise for your study, walking transects multiple times provides
little information about the spatial variability in encounter rate
through the study area for which you are drawing inference.

messages.subject: MRDS: identifying duplicate sightings
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am currently undertaking aerial surveys to estimate abundance for commo=
n dolphins in the Hauraki Gulf, New Zealand, using MRDS methods. We are r=
unning into a few issues surrounding how to identify duplicates and recon=
cile differences between duplicate records; in particular how to deal wit=
h differences in group size records between observers.=20

=46rom looking at the literature, I have found that most people have used=
 1) timing (within 5 seconds) 2) group size (plus or minus a few individu=
als) 3) angle (plus or minus 5-10 degrees), to identify duplicate sightin=
gs between observers. A sighting was considered a duplicate when two of t=
he three criteria match.

However, for common dolphins, there is huge variation in group size, and =
we often encounter groups that consist of at least ~40 to 300 individuals=
. As a result, most of the time an absolute count of the number of indivi=
duals is not possible and the discrepancy between group size estimates fr=
om two observers can be quite large.=20=20

=46rom the literature, I have found two alternative solutions. The first =
is to use the average group size when there is a difference. The second i=
s to use the larger estimate, under the assumption that under-counting th=
e number of individuals is more likely than over-counting. However, the s=
pecies in these studies typically occurred in small groups and therefore =
differences in counts were by a few individuals, rather than by 10-15 ind=
ividuals (in some cases more) as we have in our study.

A further complication is that individuals within larger groups often for=
m sub-groups that are spatially diffuse. In this case, observers on the s=
ame side of the plane may focus their attention on different sub-groups. =
However, these sub-groups may be of similar size and seen within ~5 secon=
ds but with their centers at different angles. As a result, it doesn't re=
ally make sense to use the standard criteria to identify duplicates.=20

I was wondering if anyone had faced similar problems working on similar s=
pecies, and if so, whether anyone could possibly share their solution wit=
h me?

Kind Regards,
Olivia Hamilton (oham004aucklanduni.ac.nz <http://oham004aucklanduni.ac.nz>)
PhD Candidate
Institute of Marine Science
University of Auckland

messages.subject: model and distance interval selection
messages.body_plain:
Good day,

We conducted aerial surveys over the Bangweulu Wetlands in Zambia to count Shoebills to derive a population estimate for this species. We flew line transects and counted individuals within a 200 m strip on each side of the plane, estimating the distance of the bird from the transect line.

Our data are quite straightforward, as is the analyses in Distance. The outcomes (density estimates and number of individuals) seem as expected, maybe a bit higher, but I have a few questions regarding the outcomes. I hope someone could clarify some things for me.

I ran several models at the same time (uniform with cosine and simple polynomial adjustment; half-time with cosine and simple polynomial; hazard-rate with simple polynomial. Do these models make sense?) and Distance determines the best model based on the AIC. So far so good.

However, I have selected a few different distance intervals (40 m, 50 m, 67 m) and the interval I choose has quite an effect on the outcome. How would one select between these outcomes? I believe it is the Goodness of Fit with the highest Chi-square p value? I just want to be sure I am making the right choices.

And lastly, if I select an interval of 40 m, I get very different outcomes compared to an interval of 41 m. Does anyone know why? Is it because my distance estimates are mainly in 10 m rounding and therefore this affects the outcome? The different density estimates result in quite large differences for our population estimate (15%), which, for a threatened species, could have large conservation consequences.

Thanks!

Ralf Mullers

messages.body_plain:
Ralf:

Thanks for introducing me to shoebills; interesting looking animals.

I take it you recorded exact distances to the animals you saw in the field, your binning questions relate to binning of those exact distances done during analysis.  That is my premise, I hope it is correct.

There are two places in the analysis where you can perform binning, and for very different reasons.  How to perform that binning takes place in two places in the software and discussed in two locations in the users guide as well.  It seems you are binning in both situations, i.e. binning to assess model fit to data and binning for the actual fitting of the detection function.

Without actually seeing the data, here are some speculative opinions.  If you have exact distance measurements, then you are best to use the Kolomogorov-Smirnoff goodness of fit test that does not rely upon subject decisions about cut points (as does the chi-square goodness of fit tests).  My second comment is if you are binning your data for the purposes of fitting your detection function and you are seeing considerable differences in results, this may be a result of heaping (as you describe); it may also be indicative of other challenges with the data (small sample size, spike in detection function associated with "guarding" the flightline).  With 'good' data, results are robust with respect to cut points.

Michelle:

When binning for fitting the detection function Distance will use those same bin cut-points for the chi-square GOF test.  You have essentially asked Distance to ignore the exact distances and perform both the estimation and the GOF with the use of the cut-points you have specified for your detection function fitting.  In your situation, you will need to report the chi-square GOF because, in effect, you no longer have exact distance data.
